Integrable Discretisations for a Class of Nonlinear Schrödinger Equations on Grassmann Algebras

Georgi G. Grahovski1,2 and Alexander V. Mikhailov1

1 Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Leeds, Woodhouse Lane,
Leeds, LS2 9JT, United Kingdom
2Institute of Nuclear Research and Nuclear Energy, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences,
72 Tsarigradsko chausee, Sofia 1784, Bulgaria

E-mails:     G.Grahovski@leeds.ac.uk,     A.V.Mikhailov@leeds.ac.uk

Abstract

Integrable discretisations for a class of coupled (super) nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) type of equations are presented. The class corresponds to a Lax operator with entries in a Grassmann algebra. Elementary Darboux transformations are constructed. As a result, Grassmann generalisations of the Toda lattice and the NLS dressing chain are obtained. The compatibility (Bianchi commutativity) of these Darboux transformations leads to integrable Grassmann generalisations of the difference Toda and NLS equations. The resulting systems will have discrete Lax representations provided by the set of two consistent elementary Darboux transformations. For the two discrete systems obtained, initial value and initial-boundary problems are formulated.

1 Introduction

There has been a constant interest to noncommutative extensions of integrable equations over the last few decades [7, 44, 10, 12, 16, 18, 26, 39, 40, 43, 11, 35]. Among the well-known examples are the noncommutative analogues of KdV, NLS, sine-Gordon, the KP equation, the Hirota-Miwa equation, two-dimensional Toda lattice equation and AKNS hierarchy.

Supersymmetric systems are particular examples of noncommutative extensions of integrable systems. They have attracted much attention because of their applications in physics. Perhaps the best known example of such equation is the Manin-Radul super-KdV equation [32]. It has been extensively studied by various authors [33, 38, 4, 30, 31, 25]. In [30] soliton solutions for the Manin-Radul super-KdV equation were constructed by iterating Darboux transformations, considering the cases of an even number and an odd number of iterations separately. In [29] unified formulae for the solutions not depending on the parity of the number of iterations are obtained. This is based on an alternative approach to Darboux transformations using quasi-determinants [15].

Moreover, the connections between the supersymmetric soliton equations and the theory of Lie superalgebras were analysed in [17, 37, 20], in order to obtain a super-analogue of the classical Drinfeld-Sokolov theory [13].

Darboux transformations play a crucial role in the theory of integrable systems [34]. They are gauge-like transformations which preserve the form of the associated linear problem (Lax representation) and are basic tools for obtaining the so-called soliton solutions [47, 48, 10, 9]. The theory of Darboux transformations was boosted by the dressing method [45].

Darboux transformations also play a role in constructing integrable discretisations of integrable equations [3]: to a very wide variety of (continuous) integrable nonlinear PDEs the associated dressing chains can be interpreted as Bäcklund-Darboux transformations [28]. Furthermore, the compatibility (Bianchi commutativity) of these Bäcklund-Darboux transformations leads to equations with two discrete independent variables (lattice equations). The Bianchi commutativity for Bäcklund-Darboux transformations is also known as a principle for nonlinear superposition [28]. The classifications of elementary Darboux transforms can be used as a tool to classify discrete systems related to a given Lax operator. These discrete systems will have Lax pairs provided by the set of two consistent Darboux transformations. The corresponding Bäcklund transformations will represent symmetries of the discrete (difference systems).

Here we will study Darboux transformation for a class of the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) type of systems with Lax pairs belonging to Grassmann algebras. Such systems are closely-related to the supersymmetric version of the NLS equation with an o​s​p​(1|2)osp(1|2)-invariant Lax pair studied by P. P. Kulish [24]:

i​ut+ux​x−2​u†​u​u−Ψ†​Ψ​u+i​Ψ​Ψx=0i​Ψt+Ψx​x−u†​u​Ψ+i⁡(2​u​Ψx†+Ψ†​ux)=0,\begin{split}{\rm i}u_{t}+u_{xx}-2u^{\dagger}uu-\Psi^{\dagger}\Psi u+{\rm i}\Psi\Psi_{x}=0\\ {\rm i}\Psi_{t}+\Psi_{xx}-u^{\dagger}u\Psi+{\rm i}(2u\Psi^{\dagger}_{x}+\Psi^{\dagger}u_{x})=0\end{split}, (1.1)

Here uu and Ψ\Psi are smooth functions taking values in a Grassmann algebra 𝒢=𝒢0⊕𝒢1{\mathcal{G}}={\mathcal{G}}_{0}\oplus{\mathcal{G}}_{1}. The variables uu are called commuting (bosonic) variables: u1​u2=u2​u1u_{1}u_{2}=u_{2}u_{1}, u1,u2∈𝒢0u_{1},u_{2}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{0} while the variables Ψ\Psi are called anti-commuting (fermionic) ones: Ψ1​Ψ2=−Ψ2​Ψ1\Psi_{1}\Psi_{2}=-\Psi_{2}\Psi_{1}, Ψ1,Ψ2∈𝒢1\Psi_{1},\Psi_{2}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{1}. Here also †{\dagger} stays for a Hermitian conjugation in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

The paper is organised as follows: in Section 2 we present some basic facts of Grassmann algebras, the Lax representation and the general form of the partial differential equations. In Section 3 we describe the elementary Darboux transformations and the corresponding dressing chains. In Section 4 we present the discrete integrable systems obtained as a compatibility condition of elementary Darboux transformations from Section 3.

2 Preliminaries: Grassmann algebras and Lax representation

Firstly, we present basic facts and properties of Grassmann algebras. Further details can be found e.g. in [5, 27].

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded algebra over a field KK of characteristics zero (such as ℂ{\mathbb{C}} or ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}). Thus, 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} as a linear space is a direct sum 𝒢=𝒢0⊕𝒢1{\mathcal{G}}={\mathcal{G}}_{0}\oplus{\mathcal{G}}_{1}, such that 𝒢i​𝒢j⊆𝒢i+j(mod​ 2){\mathcal{G}}_{i}{\mathcal{G}}_{j}\subseteq{\mathcal{G}}_{i+j}\quad({\rm mod}\,2). Those elements of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} that belong either to 𝒢0{\mathcal{G}}_{0} or to 𝒢1{\mathcal{G}}_{1} are called homogeneous, the ones from 𝒢0{\mathcal{G}}_{0} are called even, while those in 𝒢1{\mathcal{G}}_{1} are called odd.

By definition, the parity |a||a| of an even homogeneous element aa is 00 and it is 11 for odd homogeneous elements. The parity of the product |a​b||ab| of two homogeneous elements is a sum of their parities: |a​b|=|a|+|b||ab|=|a|+|b|. Grassmann commutativity means that b​a=(−1)|a|​|b|​a​bba=(-1)^{|a||b|}ab for any homogenous elements aa and bb. In particular, a12=0a_{1}^{2}=0, for all a1∈𝒢1a_{1}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{1} and even elements commute with all elements of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

Consider a Lax operator of the form

L=∂x+U−λh,\displaystyle L=\partial_{x}+U-\lambda h, (2.1)

Here pp and qq are even elements of the Grassmann algebra 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, while ζ\zeta, ϰ\varkappa, ϕ\phi and ψ\psi are odd homogeneous ones and λ∈ℂ\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}} is a spectral parameter (even variable). We will be using the natural grading Ui​j∈𝒢i+jU_{ij}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{i+j} (mod 22).

The zero curvature condition [L,A]=0[L,A]=0 leads to the following system of equations:

3 Darboux transforms for the Lax operator (2.1)

By a Darboux transformation we understand a map

L→L1=M​L​M−1\displaystyle L\rightarrow L_{1}=MLM^{-1} (3.1)

where the Lax operator L1L_{1} has the same form (2.1) but with an updated potential U1U_{1}:

L1=∂x+U1−λh,U1=(0ψ12​q1−ϰ10ζ12​p1ϕ10).\displaystyle L_{1}=\partial_{x}+U_{1}-\lambda h,\qquad U_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&\psi_{1}&2q_{1}\\ -\varkappa_{1}&0&\zeta_{1}\\ 2p_{1}&\phi_{1}&0\\ \end{array}\right).

In (3.1) MM is a matrix whose entries Mi​j∈𝒢i+jM_{ij}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{i+j} (mod 2) are rational functions of λ\lambda and differentiable functions of xx. It follows from (3.1) that

Mx+U1​M−M​U−λ⁡[h,M]=0.\displaystyle M_{x}+U_{1}M-MU-\lambda[h,M]=0. (3.6)

Obviously, a composition of Darboux transformations is again a Darboux transformation with more complicated rational dependence in λ\lambda.

We are interested in elementary Darboux transformations which cannot be decomposed further. Thus, we restrict ourselves by linear in λ\lambda Darboux matrices:

M=M0+λ​M1.\displaystyle M=M_{0}+\lambda M_{1}. (3.7)

The substitution of MM in (3.6) results in:

[h,M1]=0,\displaystyle[h,M_{1}]=0, (3.8)
M1,x+U1​M1−M1​U−[h,M0]=0,\displaystyle M_{1,x}+U_{1}M_{1}-M_{1}U-[h,M_{0}]=0, (3.9)
M0,x+U1​M0−M0​U=0.\displaystyle M_{0,x}+U_{1}M_{0}-M_{0}U=0. (3.10)

Let us consider the simplest case of λ\lambda- independent Darboux transformations (M1=0M_{1}=0). From (3.9) it follows that M0M_{0} is a diagonal matrix. Then, equation (3.10) implies that M0M_{0} is a constant diagonal matrix, and that U1​M0=M0​UU_{1}M_{0}=M_{0}U. The later is nothing but a Lie point symmetry transformation, which does not lead to nontrivial results.

If M1≠0M_{1}\neq 0, then it follows from (3.8) that M1M_{1} is a diagonal matrix: M1=diag​(α,β,γ)M_{1}=\mbox{diag}\,(\alpha,\beta,\gamma). Furthermore, the equation (3.9) implies that α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma are constants. We will describe the elementary Darboux transformations. In this case the matrix M1M_{1} in (3.7) has rank one and without any loss of generality, we can set α=1\alpha=1, β=0\beta=0, γ=0\gamma=0. It follows from (3.9) and (3.10) that M0,22M_{0,22} and M0,33M_{0,33} are constants. 4 Darboux transforms and discretisation

A standard approach for obtaining integrable difference equations is to construct a pair of Darboux transformations: discrete systems appear as consistency conditions of two Darboux matrices MM and NN around a square [28, 3] (the Bianchi commutativity).

Let us introduce lattice variables (k,m)(k,m) (k,m∈ℤk,m\in{\mathbb{Z}}): generic even vk,mv_{k,m} and odd variables τk,m\tau_{k,m} are defined on an integer lattice ℤ×ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{Z}} (through the whole text we adopt the convention to denote by Greek letters the odd variables and with Latin letters the even ones). It is also useful to introduce the shift operators SS and TT as follows: the operator SS shifts the first lattice variable while the operator TT shifts the second one. For example

S​qk,m=qk+1,m,T​ζk,m=ζk,m+1,T​S=S​T.\displaystyle Sq_{k,m}=q_{k+1,m},\qquad T\zeta_{k,m}=\zeta_{k,m+1},\qquad TS=ST. (4.1)

Now, consider two Darboux transformations M⁡(λ)M(\lambda) and N⁡(λ)N(\lambda). On the space of fundamental solutions {Ψ}\{\Psi\} of L⁡(λ)L(\lambda) (2.1) they act as follows:

S⁡[Ψ⁡(λ)]=M⁡(λ)​Ψ​(λ),T⁡[Ψ⁡(λ)]=N⁡(λ)​Ψ​(λ).\displaystyle S[\Psi(\lambda)]=M(\lambda)\Psi(\lambda),\qquad T[\Psi(\lambda)]=N(\lambda)\Psi(\lambda). (4.2)

The compatibility of the transformations [S,T]=0[S,T]=0 (Bianchi commutativity) implies

S⁡[N⁡(λ)]​M​(λ)=T⁡[M⁡(λ)]​N​(λ),\displaystyle S[N(\lambda)]M(\lambda)=T[M(\lambda)]N(\lambda), (4.3)

and leads to a set of algebraic relations between UU, S⁡[U]S[U], T⁡[U]T[U] and T​S​[U]TS[U].

In this setting, Darboux transformations (4.2) can be considered as a discrete Lax pair associated with L⁡(λ)L(\lambda), while the system of algebraic equations (4.3) can be considered as a system of difference equations for variables labelled by the point on the lattice. Hence, the system (4.3) is an integrable discretisation of the hierarchy of L⁡(λ)L(\lambda) having a discrete Lax pair given by (4.2). Moreover, the differential equations for the Bäcklund transformation, coming from the derivation of the Darboux matrices can be considered as symmetries of the difference system.

Here we will describe the set of integrable discretisations obtained from imposing a consistency of two Darboux transformations, obtained in the previous Section.

Case A: In this case, consider two Darboux matrices of the type described in Case 2 in section 3:

M=(μ+p10​q−ψ​ϰ10+λψq−ϰ1010p1001);N=(ν+p01​q−ψ​ϰ01+λψq−ϰ0110p0101),\displaystyle M=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\mu+p_{10}q-\psi\varkappa_{10}+\lambda&&\psi&&q\\ -\varkappa_{10}&&1&&0\\ p_{10}&&0&&1\\ \end{array}\right);\quad N=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\nu+p_{01}q-\psi\varkappa_{01}+\lambda&&\psi&&q\\ -\varkappa_{01}&&1&&0\\ p_{01}&&0&&1\\ \end{array}\right),

The consistency condition (4.3) leads to the following discrete system of four equations:

p01−p10\displaystyle p_{01}-p_{10} =\displaystyle= μ−ν(1+p11​q)2​(1+p11​q+ψ​ϰ11)​p11\displaystyle{\mu-\nu\over(1+p_{11}q)^{2}}(1+p_{11}q+\psi\varkappa_{11})p_{11}
q01−q10\displaystyle q_{01}-q_{10} =\displaystyle= −μ−ν(1+p11​q)2​(1+p11​q+ψ​ϰ11)​q\displaystyle-{\mu-\nu\over(1+p_{11}q)^{2}}(1+p_{11}q+\psi\varkappa_{11})q
ϰ01−ϰ10\displaystyle\varkappa_{01}-\varkappa_{10} =\displaystyle= μ−ν1+p11​q​ϰ11\displaystyle{\mu-\nu\over 1+p_{11}q}\varkappa_{11} (4.11)
ψ01−ψ10\displaystyle\psi_{01}-\psi_{10} =\displaystyle= −μ−ν1+p11​q​ψ\displaystyle-{\mu-\nu\over 1+p_{11}q}\psi

If all odd variables vanish, this system of difference equations reduced to a familiar two-component system [1, 2, 3]:

p01−p10=(μ−ν)​p111+p11​qq01−q10=−(μ−ν)​q1+p11​q.\displaystyle p_{01}-p_{10}={(\mu-\nu)p_{11}\over 1+p_{11}q}\qquad q_{01}-q_{10}=-{(\mu-\nu)q\over 1+p_{11}q}. (4.12)

One can easily solve (4.11) either with respect to (p10p_{10}, q10q_{10}, ψ10\psi_{10}, ϰ10\varkappa_{10}) or with respect to (p01p_{01}, q01q_{01}, ψ01\psi_{01}, ϰ01\varkappa_{01}). In this case, one can pose an initial value problem for (4.11) with initial conditions on a staircase as it is shown on Figure 1. For a given set of initial data on the staircase, a solution of the difference system (4.11) can be found recursively.

Similar to [36] one can define the Elimination map and express any variable on the lattice in terms of a finite subset of the initial set of variables on the staircase (Fig. 1). It is clear, that these expressions are rational functions of the even initial variables and multi-linear function of the odd ones.

Case B: If we combine two Darboux transformations of types (3) and (3) from the previous section:

M=(μ+p10​q−ψ​ϰ10+λψq−ϰ1010p1001),N=(F+λψq−ϰ0110p0100);\displaystyle M=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\mu+p_{10}q-\psi\varkappa_{10}+\lambda&&\psi&&q\\ -\varkappa_{10}&&1&&0\\ p_{10}&&0&&1\\ \end{array}\right),\quad N=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}F+\lambda&&\psi&&q\\ -\varkappa_{01}&&1&&0\\ p_{01}&&0&&0\\ \end{array}\right);

then the compatibility (the Bianchi commutativity) condition will lead to the following quadrilateral system:

p01\displaystyle p_{01} =\displaystyle= (μ−F+p10​q−ψ​ϰ10)​p11\displaystyle(\mu-F+p_{10}q-\psi\varkappa_{10})p_{11} (4.20)
q10\displaystyle q_{10} =\displaystyle= (μ−F10+p11​q01−ψ01​ϰ11)​q\displaystyle(\mu-F_{10}+p_{11}q_{01}-\psi_{01}\varkappa_{11})q (4.21)
ψ01−ψ10\displaystyle\psi_{01}-\psi_{10} =\displaystyle= −(μ−F10+p11​q01−ψ01​ϰ11)​ψ\displaystyle-(\mu-F_{10}+p_{11}q_{01}-\psi_{01}\varkappa_{11})\psi (4.22)
ϰ01−ϰ10\displaystyle\varkappa_{01}-\varkappa_{10} =\displaystyle= (μ−F+p10​q−ψ​ϰ10)​ϰ11\displaystyle(\mu-F+p_{10}q-\psi\varkappa_{10})\varkappa_{11} (4.23)
F⁡(μ+p11​q01−ψ01​ϰ11)\displaystyle F(\mu+p_{11}q_{01}-\psi_{01}\varkappa_{11}) =\displaystyle= F10​(μ+p10​q−ψ​ϰ10)+p10​q10−p01​q01−ψ10​ϰ10+ψ01​ϰ01,\displaystyle F_{10}(\mu+p_{10}q-\psi\varkappa_{10})+p_{10}q_{10}-p_{01}q_{01}-\psi_{10}\varkappa_{10}+\psi_{01}\varkappa_{01}, (4.24)

and the condition: p01​q=1p_{01}q=1 (3.15) which enables us to eliminate the variable pp. One can solve (4.20) and (4.21) with respect to FF and its shift F10F_{10}:

F=μ−q10q+qq1,−1−ψ​ϰ10,F10=μ−q01q+q01q10−ψ01​ϰ11.\displaystyle F=\mu-{q_{10}\over q}+{q\over q_{1,-1}}-\psi\varkappa_{10},\qquad F_{10}=\mu-{q_{01}\over q}+{q_{01}\over q_{10}}-\psi_{01}\varkappa_{11}. (4.25)

Then, using (4.25), one can eliminate FF from (4.22) and (4.23). The compatibility condition S⁡(F)=F10S(F)=F_{10} and (4.22)-(4.23) read:

qq−1,0+qq1,−1−q−1,1q−q1,0q+ψ−1,1​ξ−ψ​ξ1,−1+μ−μ1=0,\displaystyle{q\over q_{-1,0}}+{q\over q_{1,-1}}-{q_{-1,1}\over q}-{q_{1,0}\over q}+\psi_{-1,1}\xi-\psi\xi_{1,-1}+\mu-\mu_{1}=0, (4.26)

After setting q=evq={\rm e}^{v}, where vv is an even variable, one can easily recognise (4.26) as a noncommutative extension of the discrete Toda lattice:

ev1,−1−v+ev−1,0−v−ev−v1,0−ev−v−1,1+ψ−1,1​ξ−ψ​ξ1,−1+μ1−μ=0,\displaystyle{\rm e}^{v_{1,-1}-v}+{\rm e}^{v_{-1,0}-v}-{\rm e}^{v-v_{1,0}}-{\rm e}^{v-v_{-1,1}}+\psi_{-1,1}\xi-\psi\xi_{1,-1}+\mu_{1}-\mu=0, (4.29)

For the commutative Toda lattice (4.32) one can solve an initial value problem with initial data given on the staircase W0W_{0}:

W0={(k+n,m−n),(k+n,m−n−1)|n∈{0,…,2p}}.\displaystyle W_{0}=\{(k+n,m-n),(k+n,m-n-1)\,|\,n\in\{0,...,2p\}\}. (4.36)

In the case of equations (4.26) one also needs to define boundary odd variables. Taking some p∈ℕp\in{\mathbb{N}} we define a parallelogram WW (cf. Fig. 2) with boundaries

W1×\displaystyle W_{1}^{\times} =\displaystyle= {(k+2​n,m−n)|n∈{1,…,p}}\displaystyle\{(k+2n,m-n)\,|\,n\in\{1,...,p\}\} (4.37)
W1∘\displaystyle W_{1}^{\circ} =\displaystyle= {(k+2​n,m−n−p−1)|n∈{0,…,p−1}}\displaystyle\{(k+2n,m-n-p-1)\,|\,n\in\{0,...,p-1\}\} (4.38)
W2∘\displaystyle W_{2}^{\circ} =\displaystyle= {(k,m−n)|n∈{0,…,p+1}},\displaystyle\{(k,m-n)\,|\,n\in\{0,...,p+1\}\}, (4.39)
W2×\displaystyle W_{2}^{\times} =\displaystyle= {(k+2​p,m−n−p)|n∈{0,…,p+1}}.\displaystyle\{(k+2p,m-n-p)\,|\,n\in\{0,...,p+1\}\}. (4.40)

The set of boundary variables ψk​m(0)\psi_{km}^{(0)} are defined on W∘=W1∘∪W2∘W^{\circ}=W_{1}^{\circ}\cup W_{2}^{\circ} and the boundary variables ξk​m(0)\xi_{km}^{(0)} are defined on W×=W1×∪W2×W^{\times}=W_{1}^{\times}\cup W_{2}^{\times}. It is easy to show, that any variable inside the parallelogram WW bounded by W∘∪W×W^{\circ}\cup W^{\times} can be uniquely expressed as a rational function of the even variables given on the staircase W0W_{0} inscribed into the parallelogram WW and multi-linear functions of the odd variables on W∘W^{\circ} and W×W^{\times}.

Indeed, the system (4.26) with such initial boundary conditions can be solved by a finite sequence of iterations. For the first iteration we set all odd variables inside the parallelogram to zero and find the first approximation of even variables for all points of WW. Then, using the boundary conditions for odd variables, one can solve equations (4.35) to update the values of odd variables inside WW. Starting from these data, we repeat the sequence of iterations. This sequence will stabilise after a finite number of steps since the solution (qk1,m1q_{k_{1},m_{1}}, ψk1,m1\psi_{k_{1},m_{1}}, ξk1,m1\xi_{k_{1},m_{1}}), (k1,m1)∈W(k_{1},m_{1})\in W is a multi-linear function of the odd boundary data. Thus one can define again an Elimination map [36] which will allow us to express the solutions as rational functions of the even initial data on the staircase W0W_{0} inscribed into the parallelogram WW and multi-linear functions of the odd boundary data.

The mixed initial/boundary value problem presented here allows one to recover the standard staircase W0W_{0} initial value problem [3, 23] by setting ψn,m=ξn,m=0\psi_{n,m}=\xi_{n,m}=0.

5 Conclusions

In the present paper we studied integrable difference equations associated with Grassmann extensions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. We constructed two elementary Darboux transformations. As a result, new Grassmann generalisations of the Toda lattice and the NLS dressing chain are obtained. We should mention here that the noncommutative NLS dressing chain we obtained is a nonlocal one - although the commutative reduction will lead to the standard NLS dressing chain [23]. The Toda lattice dressing chain obtained here differs from the known supersymmetric Toda chains [41, 14, 6, 19].

Furthermore, we obtained difference integrable systems as a compatibility (Bianchi commutativity) of these Darboux transformations. Such systems can be viewed as Grassmann generalisations of the difference Toda and NLS equations. These lattice systems have Lax pairs provided by the set of two consistent Darboux transformations. The corresponding Bäcklund transformations represent symmetries of the discrete (difference) systems.

For the two discrete systems obtained, we formulated the initial value problems: in the first case (when two Darboux transformations with NLS-type dressing chains are combined) the well-posed initial value problem is defined (for both even and odd variables) by giving an initial profile along an infinite staircase within the (k,m)(k,m)-lattice (Fig. 1). In the second case, the well-posed initial-boundary value problem is defined for a parallelogram (of any size). The initial even variables should be given on a staircase inscribed in the parallelogram while the odd variables should be given on the boundary of the parallelogram (Fig. 2). This differs from the commutative case where the initial value problem is globally well-posed on an infinite staircase. The bosonic limit reconstructs the results of [23]. However, one can still formulate a well-posed initial value problem on a stretched staircase [21], but in the bosonic limit it will not recover the standard staircase initial value problem for the Toda lattice [3].

The results obtained here can be developed in several directions: 1) to study the corresponding Yang-Baxter maps [22, 42]; 2) To derive the recursion operators and study the associates multi-Hamiltonian structures; 3) to study Darboux transformations and the corresponding difference equations with non-evolutionary dressing chains; 4) to study elementary Darboux transformations for Lax operators with nontrivial reduction groups; 5) this can be generalised to other integrable hierarchies.
